q1.prompt: What does zero-copy mean when you access a shared dataset in Snowflake?

a.text: You query the provider's live data in place — no ETL, and no storage cost on your side
a.feedback: Correct! A shared database is a live window onto the provider's data. The provider maintains it; you don't copy, load, or pay to store it.

b.text: Snowflake copies the full dataset into your own database overnight
b.feedback: No copy is made — that's the whole point. The data stays with the provider and you query it live.

c.text: You get a one-time CSV export you load with COPY INTO
c.feedback: That's the loading pattern (Lab 7). Shared data needs no load — it's queried in place.

d.text: The dataset is stored in your account but the provider is billed for storage
d.feedback: Zero-copy means no data is stored in your account at all. The provider hosts it; you just query.

q2.prompt: A shared database called ALPINE_PEAKS_PUBLISHING already exists in your account. What single privilege does your role need to query tables inside it?

a.feedback: Correct! One GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES on the shared database unlocks all objects inside it for your role — no per-table grants needed.

b.text: SELECT granted on each table individually
b.feedback: Per-table SELECT grants work for locally-owned databases. Shared databases use IMPORTED PRIVILEGES at the database level instead.

c.feedback: You can't own a shared database — it belongs to the provider. IMPORTED PRIVILEGES is the correct consumer privilege.

d.text: ACCOUNTADMIN role — only admins can query shared databases
d.feedback: Not true. An admin grants IMPORTED PRIVILEGES to a custom role, which is exactly what the stored procedure in this lab does.

q3.prompt: A supplier wants to share their weekly price list with exactly three of their distribution partners. Which Snowflake feature fits this use case best?

a.text: Private Listing — share directly with specific invited accounts
a.feedback: Correct! A Private Listing is designed for curated, account-specific sharing. The provider invites only the accounts they choose — it's not visible on the public Marketplace.

b.text: Public Marketplace listing — publish it so anyone on Snowflake can find it
b.feedback: A public listing is visible to all Snowflake users. For a price list shared with specific partners, a Private Listing keeps it confidential.

c.text: COPY INTO — export the data as CSV files and email them to partners
c.feedback: That's a manual pipeline that creates stale copies. A Private Listing lets partners query live data with no exports or email chains.

d.text: CLONE the table into each partner's account
d.feedback: Cloning works within one account. A Private Listing is the right tool for cross-account, zero-copy distribution.

q3.prompt: You create a view in your own database that selects from a table in a privately shared database. What's true about that view?

a.text: It's still zero-copy — the view stores only its definition and reads the provider's live data on each query
a.feedback: Correct! A view stores no rows. It reads the shared table live every time, so downstream consumers get a curated, always-current interface with no extra storage.

b.text: It copies the shared rows into your database when created
b.feedback: No — a view never stores rows. It holds only the query definition and reads the underlying (shared) data at query time.

c.text: It will break the moment the provider updates their data
c.feedback: The opposite — the view always reflects the provider's current data. It only needs changing if the provider alters the columns it references.

d.text: You must own the shared database to build a view over it
d.feedback: You can't own a shared database. IMPORTED PRIVILEGES on it is enough to build a view over its tables in your own database.

q3.prompt: You acquired a privately shared database and granted your role IMPORTED PRIVILEGES. As the consumer admin, what do you control?

a.text: Which roles inside your account can read the shared database
a.feedback: Correct! The provider controls what's in the share and can revoke it; you (the consumer admin) control who inside your account can read it, by granting IMPORTED PRIVILEGES to roles.

b.text: Which tables and columns the provider includes in the share
b.feedback: That's the provider's call. As the consumer you can't add objects to the share — you only govern internal access to what's shared.

c.text: The provider's storage and compute costs for the shared data
c.feedback: The provider hosts and pays for the data. Your control is limited to who in your account may query it.

d.text: Nothing — once shared, access is fully automatic for every role
d.feedback: Not automatic. A role sees the shared database only after you grant it IMPORTED PRIVILEGES — that's exactly the control you hold.
